title: Introduction: The Bridge Between Code and Engineering
headings: The Bridge Between Code and Engineering
The two poles and the bridge
From vibe coding to specification-driven engineering
Engineering after the keyboard becomes cheap
content: The Bridge Between Code and Engineering > Choose your reading level and length above. Summary is quick; Detailed takes more time and includes more context. <Version difficulty="beginner" length="summary"> The simple version AI coding tools can build software very quickly. They can also make serious mistakes: an agent erased a production database, another product exposed payment features in the browser, and some teams shared private information with public AI tools. The problem is not that AI is always bad. The problem is trusting output that nobody has checked. Some people respond by letting AI do everything. Others refuse AI completely. Both choices give up human judgment. The safer middle path is Spec-Driven Engineering: first write what the system should do, what it must not do, and how you will test it; then ask AI to help build it; finally inspect and verify the result. The Bridge Balance teaches four stages: foundations, credible validation, AI coding agents, and autonomous agents. You do not need to write every line by hand. You do need to understand enough to specify, review, test, and own what you ship. Key idea: AI lowers the barrier to building. It does not lower the responsibility to understand. </Version> <Version difficulty="beginner" length="balanced"> The bridge in everyday language Imagine asking a very fast assistant to build a house. The assistant can carry materials and follow instructions, but it does not automatically know where the doors should go, whether the foundation is safe, or what happens in a storm. If you say only “build me a house,” you may get something that looks finished but is unsafe. AI coding agents are like that assistant. They can inspect files, write code, run commands, and change a project. They are useful, but they can guess. In 2025, a coding agent used during a Replit project deleted production data. The database contained records for about 1,206 executives and 1,196 companies. A backup eventually helped restore the data

title: Performance & Accessibility Targets
headings: Understanding speed, accessibility, and quality checks
What you can do as a content author
content: Performance & Accessibility Targets > Choose your reading level and length above. Summary is quick; Detailed lists every fix. <Version difficulty="beginner" length="summary"> The short answer We run automatic checks on every change to this site. The checks are: - Lighthouse scores the page for speed, accessibility, safety, and search visibility. - axe-core checks for barriers such as low-contrast text or missing image labels. Any change that pushes a score below its minimum is blocked until the problem is fixed. The minimums are Performance ≥ 90, Accessibility ≥ 95, Best Practices ≥ 95, and SEO ≥ 95, plus zero serious or critical accessibility violations. If you write or edit content here, add a short description, describe images, keep text readable, and keep layouts simple. That usually keeps the checks green. </Version> <Version difficulty="beginner" length="balanced"> The gate in everyday language Think of the CI pipeline as a gatekeeper that tests the website after every proposed change. Two tools run the test. Lighthouse is a web-page report card. It measures how fast the page loads, how easy it is to use with assistive tools, whether the page follows good practices, and whether it can be found by search engines. axe-core is a specialist that looks for accessibility barriers. It checks things like whether images have text descriptions, whether links have names, whether headings are ordered correctly, and whether colours have enough contrast. The numbers we require are simple: | Check | Minimum | Why | |---|---|---| | Performance | 90 | Students on ordinary laptops over Wi-Fi need a fast page | | Accessibility | 95 | The content must be usable by everyone, including with screen readers | | Best Practices | 95 | The site should be secure and avoid outdated code | | SEO | 95 | New students should be able to find the pages in search results | For accessibility, the strict rule is zero serious or critical problems. Smaller issues are recorded but do not block. When

title: Stage 1 — Spec-Aware Vibe Engineering
content: Stage 1 — Spec-Aware Vibe Engineering Foundations > Learn to lead AI coding agents with engineering judgment, not blind prompt-and-hope. This stage teaches the foundational engineering vocabulary you need to direct an AI agent confidently. The agent can write the code — your job is to know what to ask for, why, and how to know it's done right. Chapters | # | Chapter | Topic | |---|---|---| | 1 | Foundations | Software architecture: system structure, planning, architecture before code | | 2 | Core Programming | Python, JavaScript, variables, conditionals, loops, functions, file handling, error handling | | 3 | Frontend | Next.js, page structure, layouts, responsiveness, components, ShadCN / Material UI / DaisyUI | | 4 | Backend | APIs, HTTP, REST, validation, middleware, logging | | 5 | Databases | SQL vs NoSQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis, graph databases | | 6 | Git & GitHub | Commits, branches, pull requests, repos, collaboration | Learning outcomes By the end of Stage 1 you will be able to: 1. Sketch a system's architecture on a whiteboard before asking an agent to build it. 2. Read code in Python or JavaScript and identify the constructs being used. 3. Describe what a frontend component, a backend endpoint, and a database table each do — and which one a problem belongs to. 4. Use Git and pull requests to keep your work traceable and reviewable. How this stage is taught Each chapter pairs a video lecture (the primary medium) with this text companion (the second medium, for reference and search). Lecture content is delivered separately and pasted into the chapter files here. > The text is the documentation; the video is the lecture. Both are required.
